issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Situations: Sexual situations or intimacy
issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old married male ship captain with a man-made disaster trauma, 'sexual situations or intimacy' is a hard-to-explain trigger unless the disaster had a sexual/interpersonal component, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items (object throwing, uniforms) fit danger/aggression themes, making this item stand out as clinically incongruent with the trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: 'Sexual coping' appears to be organized around the same sexualized theme as the sexual trigger, but that theme is otherwise absent from Threat, Negative Appraisals, and the disaster trauma context. In this profile it does not cohere with the dominant formulation of external danger, mistrust, and vigilance, whereas dropping responsibilities and gambling are more plausibly linked to avoidance/arousal management.

vignette:
Thomas Brennan's Testimony

Thomas Brennan was forty-two years old when the cargo vessel Pacific Star caught fire in international waters off the coast of Baja California. He had been captain for seven years, a promotion he'd earned through meticulous attention to protocol and an almost obsessive knowledge of every system aboard his ship. The morning of the incident, he was in the wheelhouse reviewing manifests when the first explosion tore through the lower decks. The sound was not what he had imagined explosions to be-not a single crack, but a rolling, layered detonation that seemed to come from everywhere at once, rattling his bones and the steel around him. In the chaos that followed, a crew member beside him had panicked and hurled a wrench across the bridge in frustration; it had struck the navigation console inches from Thomas's head. He remembered the particular weight of that moment-the helplessness of being trapped in a metal tube filling with smoke, the knowledge that the emergency protocols he'd drilled a hundred times were failing, and the sickening realization that the fire had started because of a falsified maintenance log. Someone in the company's office, someone he would never meet, had signed off on inspections that were never performed.

The ship was evacuated successfully, and no lives were lost. Thomas had done his job. But in the months that followed, something had shifted in him. When he returned to work six weeks later, he found himself unable to trust the reports submitted by his crew. He began conducting his own redundant inspections, staying awake through the night to verify that safety systems were actually operational. The exhaustion accumulated. He stopped sleeping normally, his mind refusing to let his guard down even in the safety of his cabin. He would lie in bed beside his wife, Margaret, acutely aware of where the exits were, calculating whether he could reach the door quickly enough if something went wrong. He began choosing which side of the bed to sleep on based on proximity to the cabin entrance.

Within months, Thomas had stepped down from active captaincy. He told his company that he needed a shore-based role, and they accommodated him-he'd been a valuable employee for years. But the truth was that he had become convinced that he could not rely on anyone to do their jobs properly, that the entire maritime industry was run by people who cut corners and falsified records. More troubling was the fear that had begun to crystallize: if he thought too carefully about what had happened, if he allowed himself to fully imagine the fire spreading, the ship going down, the crew drowning, he would not be able to contain his reaction. He had begun to avoid even reading incident reports or watching news coverage of maritime accidents. When his mind drifted toward those memories, he would abruptly change the subject or, in the evenings, sit at his computer and spend hours gambling on offshore poker sites. The gambling gave him something to focus on, a sense of control and the occasional rush of winning that drowned out the intrusive images.

His world had contracted. He refused invitations to restaurants or social venues he hadn't visited before, unable to assess the safety of unfamiliar spaces. He found himself watching people carefully when they were near him-scanning for signs of instability or recklessness. When he heard a loud noise, a car backfiring or a door slamming, his body would go rigid. The sight of a police officer or coast guard uniform in public would send a spike of adrenaline through him, though he could not fully articulate why.

Margaret had noticed the changes, of course. She had watched her husband withdraw from the life they'd built together, had seen him decline social invitations and spend evenings hunched over his laptop. She had suggested therapy, but Thomas had resisted. What he feared most was not the memories themselves but what would happen if he allowed them to surface. He was certain that acknowledging the full weight of that day-the explosion, the wrench, the realization that his company had lied-would break something in him that could not be repaired. What finally brought him to his first appointment was not his own conviction but a conversation with Margaret one evening, when she told him that she felt like she was living with a stranger, and that she couldn't watch him disappear any longer. It was her ultimatum, delivered with tears, that made him pick up the phone.
